notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment reversing summary judgment; oral agreement for panel referral is arguable.

enrichment.short_title: Reeds v Norwich Union: summary judgment on oral lead-solicitor referral agreement
key_facts: Reeds Solicitors claimed Norwich Union and Hill House Hammond orally agreed to refer about 80% of legal expenses insurance cases for five years after joint venture talks collapsed.
Written panel, services and consultancy agreements with BTE LawLine and related companies contained entire agreement clauses and no percentage referral term.
Norwich Union applied for summary judgment on the basis that no realistic prospect existed of proving the alleged oral agreement.
Miss Reed's witness statement described confirmations at Hilton Metropole meetings in late 2002 that the firm would receive in excess of 80% of claims for five years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment striking out the solicitors' claim for breach of contract against Norwich Union and associated defendants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the claim had a realistic prospect of success and should proceed to trial, with costs deferred.
enrichment.ratio: Where an oral agreement is alleged alongside subsequent written contracts with entire agreement clauses, summary judgment is inappropriate if the claimant's evidence, read as a whole, could support either a partly oral contract or a collateral promise at the time the written agreements were signed.
legal_issues: Whether there was no realistic prospect of proving an oral agreement for 80% case referrals
Whether separate claims could be brought against Norwich Union, Hill House Hammond and BTE LawLine
Whether entire agreement clauses and non-binding comfort letters defeated the oral agreement case
Whether the judge erred in treating omissions in the witness statement as fatal to the claim

confidence.notes: Full appellate reasoning on summary judgment disposal; merits remain untried.

notes: Section 288 planning challenge; Inspector's removal of agricultural occupancy condition upheld on both grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Epping Forest v SoS: challenge to removal of agricultural occupancy condition
key_facts: The Elms at Pick Hill, Waltham Abbey, was subject to a 1950 agricultural occupancy condition in the Green Belt.
Mr and Mrs Emery applied to remove the condition after failing to sell the property; the council refused but an Inspector allowed the appeal in July 2004.
The Inspector found no demand for an occupier satisfying the condition despite extensive marketing at discounts of 22% to 30% off open market value.
Epping Forest District Council challenged the Inspector's decision under section 288 on demand and pricing grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court section 288 application to quash an Inspector's decision deleting an agricultural occupancy condition.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Inspector lawfully concluded the condition had outlived its usefulness and the council's challenges on demand and marketing price failed.
enrichment.ratio: An Inspector need not state a precise realistic price for a dwelling with an agricultural occupancy condition where, on the evidence of a sustained marketing exercise, there was no demand at any price reasonably payable by a qualifying purchaser; a single 'in any event' finding on holdings with dwellings does not vitiate the overall demand conclusion.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector's demand finding was perverse or unsupported by evidence
Whether the Inspector failed to determine if the asking price reflected an appropriate discount for the occupancy condition
Application of PPG7 and local plan policy GB17 to removal of occupancy conditions
Whether Nicholson v Secretary of State required a specific realistic price determination
linked_authorities: Nicholson v Secretary of State for the Environment [1998] JPL 553

confidence.notes: Detailed final judgment disposing of both grounds with clear reasoning on market value and demand.

notes: Housing benefit overpayment recovery; Commissioner wrongly substituted his own fact-finding for the tribunal's.

enrichment.short_title: Braintree v Thompson: housing benefit recovery after contrived tenancy finding
key_facts: Mr Thompson, a councillor and landlord, and his tenant Mr Unsworth were convicted of conspiring to defraud the council by falsely claiming the tenant lived alone at 23 Trafalgar Court.
The council sought recovery of £16,196.57 housing benefit overpaid from August 1995 to October 1999 on the basis of a contrived tenancy.

The Social Security Appeal Tribunal upheld the overpayment; Deputy Commissioner Mark allowed Mr Thompson's appeal, finding the scam targeted council tax and income support rather than housing benefit.
Crown Court evidence showed less benefit would have been paid if shared occupation had been declared.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Deputy Commissioner's decision setting aside a Social Security Appeal Tribunal's overpayment determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Commissioner's interference with the tribunal's fact-finding was erroneous in law and the tribunal's decision was restored.
enrichment.ratio: A Commissioner may set aside a tribunal decision only on a question of law; where there was abundant evidence from the criminal trial that less housing benefit would have been paid if the true shared occupation had been known, the Commissioner could not substitute his own view of the facts even if microfiche records suggested benefit levels had not increased after the pretended move-out.
legal_issues: Whether liability was created to take advantage of the housing benefit scheme under regulation 7
Whether the Commissioner exceeded his powers by deciding issues of fact
Effect of criminal conviction and Crown Court summing-up on social security appeal proceedings
Whether the council suffered prejudice because less benefit would have been paid
linked_authorities: Reg. v Hillingdon L.B.C., Ex P. Pulhofer [1986] 1 A.C. 484

confidence.notes: Complex factual background but clear appellate ruling restoring the tribunal on law/fact distinction.

notes: Lord Bingham on forfeiture vs restoration routes for seized dutiable goods; Gora/Gascoyne res judicata applied.

enrichment.short_title: Customs v VAT Tribunal: restoration after condemnation of seized cigarettes
key_facts: Mr Eatock and Mr Speakman imported large quantities of cigarettes through Blackpool Airport in November 2000; the goods and a car were seized as liable to forfeiture.
Magistrates condemned the goods as forfeited after hearings in October 2001 and, following disputed reopening, again in March 2002.
The VAT and Duties Tribunal directed a fresh Customs review, finding the imports were not for a commercial purpose.
Mr Turner's car was deemed forfeited after he failed to serve a timely notice of claim; the Tribunal held non-restoration unreasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal against VAT and Duties Tribunal decisions on restoration of goods and a vehicle seized by Customs.
enrichment.outcome: Eatock and Speakman appeals dismissed and the Tribunal's orders stood; Turner's appeal allowed and the matter remitted for reassessment of hardship.
enrichment.ratio: Where goods have been condemned in forfeiture proceedings, the restoration route cannot reopen facts necessarily decided or impliedly found by the Magistrates' Court; a Tribunal hearing a section 16(4) ancillary matter must apply the unreasonableness standard and cannot substitute its own merits review.
legal_issues: Distinction between the forfeiture route and the restoration route under CEMA
Whether prior Magistrates' Court condemnation precludes reopening commercial purpose under Gora and Gascoyne
Validity of a purported rehearing in the Magistrates' Court after the first condemnation orders
Scope of Tribunal powers under Finance Act 1994 section 16(4) on ancillary restoration decisions
linked_authorities: Gora v Customs & Excise Commissioners [2003] 3 WLR 160
Gascoyne v Customs & Excise Commissioners [2005] 2 WLR 222
Regina (Hoverspeed Ltd) v Customs & Excise Commissioners [2002] 3 WLR 1219

confidence.notes: Long procedural judgment with some unresolved factual gaps about Tribunal disclosure but clear final disposals.

notes: Presumed undue influence in family property deed; transaction explicable without shifting burden to father.

enrichment.short_title: Turkey v Awadh: presumed undue influence over leasehold transfer deed
key_facts: Aziza and Adnan Awadh purchased 141 Inverness Terrace on mortgage and let it to Aziza's father Khalid at £1,500 per month.
In May 1993 they executed a deed requiring Khalid to pay 500,000 Saudi Riyals immediately and discharge the mortgage before transfer of the leasehold interest.
Khalid paid the Riyals and later cleared the mortgage, seeking specific performance; Aziza and Adnan pleaded misrepresentation and undue influence.
The judge found a relationship of trust and confidence but rejected misrepresentation and held the transaction did not call for explanation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a 13-day Chancery county court trial refusing to set aside a family property transfer deed for presumed undue influence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the deed was enforceable because the transaction was explicable by ordinary family motives and the presumption of undue influence did not arise.
enrichment.ratio: Under Etridge, presumed undue influence requires both a relationship of trust and confidence and a transaction calling for explanation; a family arrangement to rescue mortgagors from repossession by paying cash upfront and delaying transfer until the mortgage is cleared may be explicable without inferring abuse of influence, even where no independent advice was given.
legal_issues: Whether a parent-daughter relationship of trust and confidence existed
Whether failure to assess property value made the transaction call for explanation
Application of Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) and Macklin v Dowsett
Whether the burden shifted to Khalid to rebut presumed undue influence
linked_authorities: Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2002] 2 AC 773

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate endorsement of unchallenged trial findings on Etridge analysis.

notes: Selhurst Park lease trial on rent, ground-sharing and season ticket accounting; comprehensive final judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Altonwood v Crystal Palace: Selhurst Park turnover rent and ground-sharing lease
key_facts: Altonwood leased Selhurst Park Stadium to Crystal Palace FC (2000) Ltd for ten years from July 2000 with basic rent of £156,000 and turnover rent of 10% of gross gate receipts.
A ground-sharing licence with Wimbledon FC reduced turnover rent to 7.5% while the licence subsisted and required licence fees to be paid to the landlord.
After Wimbledon vacated under a 2003 operation agreement, disputes arose over whether the licence still triggered the reduced rate and over Play-Off semi-final receipts.
Crystal Palace had paid turnover rent including sums later accepted as wrongly calculated for complimentary tickets.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary and substantive issues on construction of a football stadium lease after summary judgment was refused.
enrichment.outcome: Licence ceased to subsist as a ground-sharing agreement after the 2003 operation agreement; Play-Off match was a League Match; overpayments creditable against future turnover rent but not basic rent; season tickets calculated on receipts not accruals basis.
enrichment.ratio: A ground-sharing licence stripped of all use rights ceases to 'subsist' for turnover rent reduction purposes; 'without deduction or set-off' clauses exclude equitable set-off but clause 5.1.2 permits credit for turnover overpayments; gross gate receipts for season tickets fall due when received, not spread on an accruals basis.
legal_issues: Whether the Wimbledon licence continued to subsist after the 2003 operation agreement
Whether breach of clause 5.13.4 gave rise to recoverable damages
Whether the May 2004 Sunderland Play-Off match was a League Match or Cup Match
Whether erroneous turnover payments could be set off against basic rent
linked_authorities: Federal Commerce & Navigation Company Limited v Molena Alpha Inc [1978] QB 927
Connaught Limited v Indoor Leisure Limited [1994] 1 WLR 501

confidence.notes: Full trial judgment with detailed lease construction and clear holdings on each live issue.

notes: Contractual construction of manager severance on relegation; footballing reality preferred over share membership.

enrichment.short_title: Manchester City v Royle: severance pay after Premier League relegation
key_facts: Joe Royle's June 2000 contract as Manchester City manager provided four years' employment with tiered basic salary and bonuses by division.
Clause 14.3 required 12 months' gross basic salary on early termination if the first team was 'in the Premier League' but only six months if 'in the First Division'.
City finished third from bottom in May 2001 and dismissed Royle on 21 May before Premier League share transfer formalities completed.
The club paid six months at First Division rates; Royle claimed 12 months at Premier League rates.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Mercantile Court judgment construing a football manager's contractual severance clause.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; on dismissal after relegation at season end the club was in the First Division for clause 14.3 purposes and only six months' compensation was payable.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 14.3 was a broad-brush proxy for common law wrongful dismissal damages keyed to the manager's prospective earnings; where dismissal followed relegation at the end of the season, 'in the Premier League' means the division in which the club would actually play, not formal shareholding membership pending transfer.
legal_issues: Whether 'in the Premier League' meant shareholding membership or footballing status after relegation
Purpose of clause 14.3 as a proxy for assessment of wrongful dismissal damages
Interaction with Premier League rules B.3 to B.5 on relegation and share transfer
Commercial sense of rewarding a manager after relegation at Premier League rates
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

confidence.notes: Clear appellate reasoning resolving ambiguous contractual wording by commercial purpose.

notes: Part IV Children Act fact-finding; threshold established by finding mother caused child's death.

enrichment.short_title: Re K: care proceedings finding mother caused toddler's death
key_facts: Care proceedings concerned a three-year-old subject child whose older siblings L and H had died in 2003 and 2004 while in the mother's sole care.
L aged three years nine months died on 2 February 2004 with a forehead cut, back bruising and neck marks; H's cause of death was not determined.
Medical experts excluded infection and favoured non-accidental neck compression causing airway and venous obstruction.
The mother gave an account of events that the judge found incomplete and inaccurate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part IV Children Act 1989 fact-finding hearing before Charles J to determine threshold criteria.
enrichment.outcome: The court found on the balance of probabilities that the mother inflicted neck compression causing L's death and injuries, establishing the threshold criteria.
enrichment.ratio: Where expert evidence excludes natural causes and points to inflicted neck compression coinciding with other injuries, and the mother's account of the day's events is unreliable, the civil standard supports a finding that the sole carer caused the child's death for threshold purposes under the Children Act 1989.
legal_issues: Cause of L's death and whether inflicted injury was more likely than accidental or natural causes
Reliability of the mother's account of events on 2 February 2004
Whether threshold significant harm criteria were satisfied
Appropriate use of expert medical and pathology evidence in fact-finding

confidence.notes: Very long anonymised fact-finding judgment; core threshold finding and medical reasoning are clearly stated.

notes: Rent review construction; landlord's exclusive right to trigger open review upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Hemingway v Clothworkers: landlord-only open rent review clause
key_facts: A 1972 deed extended a 1953 lease of 3 Copthall Avenue to 2033 and introduced open rent reviews every seven years from 24 June 1982 at 60% of open market rack rental value.
Reviews in 1982 and 1989 increased rent to £229,200 and then £375,000; the landlords declined to initiate further reviews.
The tenant sought a mandatory 2003 review arguing an open clause could not be rendered upwards-only by landlord veto.
The tenant alternatively contended unrevised rent reverted to the 1982 figure if no review occurred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations on construction of rent review provisions in a deed of variation.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the lessor alone could elect whether to review and unrevised rent continued at the last reviewed figure until the term ended.
enrichment.ratio: There is no general presumption that open rent review clauses must be mandatory or exercisable by both parties; clear language giving the lessor alone the right to review prevails even without an upwards-only ratchet, and failure to review does not revert rent to an earlier baseline.
legal_issues: Whether the tenant could compel a rent review under clause 5(3)
Effect of the definition of 'appropriate percentage' if no review was implemented
Commercial purpose of rent review clauses versus express landlord option
Distinction between operative provisions and review machinery

notes: Medical negligence causation appeal; retrial ordered after undisclosed expert literature mischaracterised.

enrichment.short_title: Breeze v Ahmad: GP negligence causation retrial after expert literature error
key_facts: Leonard Breeze died aged 56 on 20 July 1999 from hypertensive and ischaemic heart disease after chest pain on 22 June 1999.
His GP Dr Ahmad did not physically examine him and diagnosed musculoskeletal pain; the trial judge found breach of duty.
Post-mortem showed severe coronary atherosclerosis with about 90% luminal occlusion and left ventricular hypertrophy.
On causation the judge preferred Dr Channer's evidence supported by Lancet studies Monica and RITA-3, which were not before the court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission of the trial judge against dismissal of a clinical negligence claim after findings of breach but not causation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; causation remitted to HHJ McKenna for retrial because the judge relied on mischaracterised expert literature never produced at trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge materially prefers one expert's causation evidence based on literature summaries taken on trust but neither party produced the papers and the summaries were inaccurate or incomplete, the resulting preference constitutes a serious procedural irregularity warranting retrial of causation.
legal_issues: Whether hospital referral would on the balance of probabilities have prevented sudden cardiac death
Admissibility and use of epidemiological literature in expert cardiac evidence
Whether the judge's preference for Dr Channer over Professor Oakley was procedurally unfair
Appropriate directions for expert literature under CPR Part 35 on remittal
linked_authorities: Wardlaw v Farrar [2004] Lloyd's Rep Med 98

confidence.notes: Breach finding undisturbed; appellate order remits causation only with clear procedural reasoning.
